title: How two people with no gamedev experience made our first Steam game with AI assistance
author: DepartmentPlus5191
selftext:
Hi, I'm Hop from Nibble & Hop, a small indie game team from Korea.

I got into the game industry because I wanted to design and make games with my own hands, and it finally feels like I've taken the first step toward that dream. I thought it would take much longer, but the AI era arrived sooner than anyone expected, and it helped me get there a little faster :)

Today I want to write down how we made our first game with the help of AI, including the parts that didn't go so well.

  
We both have day jobs, and neither of us had any real game development experience when we started. I majored in programming, but I never worked as a developer after graduating, so I only had the basics. Nibble had worked as a planner in the subculture space, but had never designed a game before.

  
I started seriously learning AI tools around last October, and in November we put together our first team. It was a visual novel project with an artist, a developer, and Nibble as the scenario writer. But as the project dragged on, the artist stepped away first, the dev side got busy with their own lives, and the team naturally drifted apart.

  
After that, I tried making a mobile idle game on my own. I got it to a basic playable state, but I decided that bringing it up to a releasable level would cost far too much, so I stopped. Then life got busy and I stepped away from making games for a while.

  
Then Nibble came to me with an idea and asked if I wanted to make a game together again. That's how our current project started, at the end of July this year.

https://preview.redd.it/lc7i9n8dwcrh1.png?width=815&format=png&auto=webp&s=4690c6909b1d2a358c348d726f9e2f5f1927892f

Since neither of us had game design experience, I first built a tool for game planning, and Nibble drafted the design document using it. The image below is a hand-drawn sketch with notes from our very first brainstorming session. Small barred windows, old and damaged wallpaper... we set the mood of the game right from this stage.

  
My coding skills weren't good enough to write everything by hand, and we had no artist, so we agreed to use AI as much as possible. That said, the core game ideas and the entire story were written by us.

Here's what we used: Claude Code and Codex for code, Gemini Nano Banana for art, Suno for sound, Qwen for Chinese language support, and Wan for video generation. The engine is Godot.

Our workflow was this loop, over and over:  
Organize the design with AI → generate code → human QA → fix the code → human QA again

  
To be honest, there wasn't really anything where AI went beyond our expectations. Going in, we expected it could get things to about 80%, and that turned out to be exactly right... which meant every single area still needed human hands.

I edited the tracks Suno generated myself. Nibble and I fixed up every image from Nano Banana by hand in Photoshop. I also designed and polished the UI myself, working from basic design elements. AI was a tool for getting a starting point quickly, not a tool for making a finished product.

  
And now, *In Your Hands* is coming to Steam soon. It's a psychological horror sound novel (a narrative game where sound drives the atmosphere) about a child who wakes up with no memories in a ruined building and explores a strange, unsettling place.

If you could add it to your wishlist, it would mean a lot to a tiny team like ours.  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5193580/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5193580/)

If you're also developing in a small team or using AI in your workflow, I'd love to hear how you work. Feel free to ask me anything too! :)

Thanks for reading this long post! :)
